segments.voice: Yesterday, reading the Gita's first chapter: svajana, one's own people, and lines that draw the circle as wide as the earth. This week ran from aham, I, to that wide circle.

Before answering a text that stings, there's a moment: it's been read, and nothing's typed yet. The Gita's second verse lives in that moment. After the blind king's question, Sanjaya's report turns to Duryodhana, the prince on the other side, and his first move isn't speech. Some people answer in seconds; some sit on it. Duryodhana, at the opening of a war, sits on it for one word. It's a look. The verse opens with one word: drishtva. Having seen.
screen: `READ, NOT YET TYPED.` → `SANJAYA TURNS TO DURYODHANA.` → `DRISHTVA: HAVING SEEN.`

segments.voice: The verse: drishtva tu pandavanikam vyudham duryodhanas tada, acharyam upasangamya raja vachanam abravit. Drishtva: the ending -tva means having done it. Having seen the Pandava army. Vyudham, drawn up in formation. Upasangamya: having gone up to his teacher. Acharyam, the teacher. Raja, king: the title the verse gives Duryodhana. Abravit: he spoke, waiting at the very end. Having seen, having gone up, he spoke. The look comes first; the words come last. Now the week, round by round. Aham, tvam, ime, vayam: I, you, these, and we, all of us, the circle Krishna closes. Atman, the self that can be its own friend or its own enemy. Maya, appearance to one school and God's real power to another, each heard at its best. Pashyan, shvasan: the body's verbs, while seeing, while breathing, each one marked by -an. Yuyutsavah, wanting to fight, and jijnasa, wanting to know: one pattern, two wantings. Svajana, one's own people, and a line that widens the family to the earth. A week of small words, and now a real chapter, read in its own language, one verse at a time. The prince has looked. Next, the chapter's people start to talk, and some of what they say has an edge.
screen: `DRISHTVA: HAVING SEEN.` · `ABRAVIT: HE SPOKE, LAST.` · `A WEEK OF SMALL WORDS.` · `FROM AHAM TO SVAJANA.` · then, large: `LOOK FIRST. THE VERB WAITS.`

segments.voice: Sit up with both feet on the floor, and before anything else, look: let your eyes move slowly around the room and take it in, the way the verse puts seeing first. Then rest your gaze on one spot and stay with the breath, looking before any speaking, even the speaking inside. If your eyes land on a person, or a photo of one, let them be seen before anything is said about them.
Reading the Gita's first chapter: today, drishtva, having seen, the -tva ending that puts a look before a word. Two verbs of having done, then one of doing.
Your line: reading the Gita's first chapter in the original. Look first; the verb waits at the end. A week, and a verse.

fork.setup: you meet a Sanskrit line with three verbs: two end in -tva or -ya, and one at the end looks finished. which is the main action?
fork.reveal: the -tva and -ya words are having-dones; the main verb, like abravit, he spoke, waits at the end.
